title: Practical coordination patterns for routing and cache invalidation
body:
Purpose:
This is a practical (working) note capturing lightweight coordination patterns we can use in the control plane and data plane to keep routing decisions correct across regions while minimizing latency and operational complexity. Focus is on: 1) what state belongs in strongly consistent stores, 2) pragmatic cache invalidation strategies, and 3) hedging/fallback routing policies for degraded regions.

Context and constraints (quick):
- Redwood needs sub-100ms p95 routing decisions in hosted mode for most customers (edge admission + model pinning).
- Control plane must be multi-region for availability and locality; cannot force every read to a single global leader without big latency cost.
- Some state is small and hot (route->backend mappings, model pins, rollout flags). Other state is large and cold (audit history, long tail configs).
- We prefer operational simplicity over theoretical purity — patterns should be testable and reversible.

High-level principle: carve state by criticality and mutation frequency
- Strong-consistency candidates (store in strongly-consistent store like etcd/CRDB with leader semantics):
  - Ownership / lease records used for routing that must not be split-brain (e.g., node/session ownership for dedicated machines).
  - Cluster-wide configuration flags that drive safety-critical behavior (emergency kill-switch, global capacity throttle).
  - Short-lived leader elections and leases (TTL short, ~10s) where a stale value causes correctness violations.

- Relaxed-consistency candidates (cache-first; background convergence acceptable):
  - Per-customer routing preferences and model-version hints (can be stale for a few seconds).
  - Observability annotations, cost heuristics, per-route metrics.
  - Non-critical rollout metadata (experiment labels, telemetry sampling rates).

Design pattern: lease-anchored cache + tombstone-driven invalidation
- Primary record lives in CRDB/etcd (we prefer lightweight etcd for small records; use CRDB where we need SQL queries and multi-row transactions).
- Cache copies live in regional in-memory caches (sidecars or local kv stores). Each cached entry carries: value, origin-version, lease-expiry, tombstone-ttl (if deleted).
- Writes: write to primary store + bump a monotonically increasing revision (etcd-style modRevision or CRDB sequence). Return revision to caller.
- Invalidation propagation: a tiny invalidation feed streams revision deltas (not full objects) to regions. Regions apply if revision > local_revision. If a region misses feed packets, it requests a compacted snapshot or falls back to origin read.

Why tombstones?
- Delete operations are common (model unpin, deprovision) and we need a cheap way to indicate ‘‘gone’’ until caches can evict safely. Tombstone carries a TTL (e.g., 60s) that gives caches a predictable window to evict. After TTL expiry a compact job cleans tombstones.

Cache eviction heuristics and read flow
- Strong read path for routing: local cache lookup -> if found and lease not expired, use it. If lease expired or tombstone present, async refresh + use fallback routing (see fallback policies).
- Background refresh: on lease expiry, region tries a non-blocking fetch from control plane; if fetch succeeds quickly (<= 50ms) update cache and continue; otherwise, use fallback decision.
- Eviction policies align with traffic shape: prefer LRU with explicit size caps per customer to avoid noisy neighbors.

Fallback routing (safety + QoE tradeoffs)
- Goals: keep request success high, avoid unsafe routing (e.g., sending private-customer traffic to wrong model), and bound tail latency.
- Candidate fallback policies (in order of preference):
  1) Soft-fallback: route to a region-local compatible model variant (same family + lower capacity) with a failover tag. Record a telemetry event for automatic reconciliation.
  2) Hedged read: if local cache missing, initiate a hedged fetch to origin + attempt local fallback; if origin wins quickly, use it; otherwise, complete fallback. Limit to 1 hedged attempt per request to cap cost.
  3) Proxy-through-origin: for requests where correctness matters more than latency, proxy request to control plane region (use sparingly; only in dedicated customer SLOs).

Multi-region replication topology choices and tradeoffs
- Option A: Active/Active read cache + single-writer per-tenant (preferred):
  - Each tenant is pinned to a write-region for control plane mutations (lease owner). Reads are local.
  - Pro: low read latency, no global serialization for reads. Con: writes have cross-region latency for non-write-region clients; need fast invalidation feed.

- Option B: Global linearizable store (single logical leader)
  - Strong correctness but high latency for global writes; operationally simpler for developers.

- Option C: Workload-split (some tables in global store, others regional)
  - Use strongly-consistent store for critical rows, and regional stores for high-cardinality low-criticality data. Adds operational complexity but reduces latency.

Store selection heuristics (etcd vs CRDB vs cloud-managed KVS)
- Use etcd when: small records, heavy watch semantics, we need efficient revision-based watches and TTL leases. Good for cluster/instance ownership, leader election, ephemeral leases.
- Use CRDB when: we need relational queries, secondary indexes, or multi-row transactional updates (e.g., rollout batch updates across many routes).
- Use managed cloud KVS (Dynamo-like) when: very high fanout config that tolerates eventual consistency and we want cheaper scaling (e.g., feature flags with 100k customers).

Operational patterns and safeguards
- Safe rollout for cache invalidation changes: launch invalidation change in canary region -> monitor stale hits metric -> gradually ramp to other regions.
- Alerting: high ratio of served-stale-cache events or tombstone-expiry counts should trigger runbook that forces a snapshot sync.
- Admin override: admin writes to a tightly-consistent path that increments an emergency revision; regions subscribe and immediately evict caches on receive. This gives a single-button safety kill.

Instrumentation & data for tuning
- Emit these metrics per-region/per-tenant: cache-hit-rate, cache-stale-hit-rate, tombstone-hit-rate, watch-lag-ms (how far behind the latest revision), hedged-read-rate, fallback-route-rate, origin-read-latency.
- Keep short TTL traces for hedged requests (did origin win? how often?).

Examples (pseudo-config snippets)
- Cached entry metadata (conceptual):
  - key: customer/route/123
  - value: {backend: model-a-v3, rev: 16784, lease_expiry_ts: 1700000000, tombstone: false}
- Invalidation event payload (small): {key: customer/route/123, rev: 16785, type: update|delete}

Open questions / TODOs
- What is our acceptable tombstone TTL by customer tier? (enterprise vs free) -- proposal: enterprise 10s, standard 60s, free 120s. Need empirical test.
- How often will regions miss invalidation feed under sustained GCs / network blips? Add chaos tests to measure.
- Backpressure and runaway hedging: need per-node hedging budgets to avoid amplification.
- Test matrix: write correctness tests for concurrent write scenarios when a tenant is actively being rolled out in 3 regions.

Suggested experiments (short term)
- Canary an invalidation feed consumer that uses revision-only deltas (not full snapshots) in west-eu and measure watch-lag and snapshot-fallback rates over 48h.
- Inject tombstones for a set of routes and measure user-visible error rate and reconciliation time.

Notes to self / rough plan
- Iterate: implement small revision-only invalidation stream -> light client-side cache with lease expiry -> hedged-read as opt-in per-tenant -> collect metrics -> tune TTLs.
- Keep API for admin immediate-evict.

References/links (internal):
- See PLAT-1423 for tenant pinning requirements.
- Routing proto PR (above) contains initial invalidation event schema.

End (working document).

Unresolved: whether we should use etcd for high-cardinality tenant routing entries (scale concerns). If we decide not to, document an eventual migration path (compact snapshots + cheap lease metadata in etcd, payloads in S3-backed store).

-- Leah
